Can you tell us more about the condition in which you found these people? You told us that you, yourself, were fearful in there. What condition did you find these people in?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I said, when I entered that small room, in one corner, there was a large group of prisoners; and in the other, a smaller group. They were packed tight together and seated on the floor. They were obviously very scared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're saying they were attached together. They were attached together, you were saying?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, huddled together. I didn't even notice if they were restrained in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have told us already that they were restrained, but you don't know whether they were tied in front or at the back, their hands?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I meant both groups. I'm not sure if all of them were restrained. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Again, sir, this is again what surprises me. What had you gone to do there as a person responsible for the security? Why did you bother to go to that building, if you can't remember the condition in which you found these people?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just tried to see them, to talk to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: With what purpose in mind, what for?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simply to see them, to take their details, to record them; however, I was soon bruskily interrupted and driven away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But let me just find out, sir, with respect to prisoners of war, what were your responsibilities as an official in the army responsible for security?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the military police who were responsible for taking them to the reception centre in Zenica, at least according to the procedure. Whenever there were prisoners, it was the job of the military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt that answer because it's not answering my question. Can you please answer my question? I can repeat it, if you want me to.

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it was my responsibility to take them there or hand them over to the reception centre; me personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Again, sir, you are not answering my question. Please answer my question. Do you want me to repeat my question?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm saying, as an official responsible for security in the army, what, if any, were your responsibilities vis a vis prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The responsibilities of the security organ were to coordinate police work, to direct police work in that activity as well, taking POWs to wherever they were being taken to. What could I do? I could record their names. I could inform my superior officer, who could then possibly enlist the assistance of the military police so that they could wrap up the job. That was my understanding of my own role.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me ask you the same question slightly differently. Was it not part of your responsibility, sir, when you go and see prisoners of war, wherever they may be, to make a specific note of their condition?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote down what I saw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is it that you wrote down, sir? What is it that you saw?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, when I saw them, they were scared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's why I said, "in what condition were they?"

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure how else to put this. They were scared, huddled together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's all you can remember about them, about their condition?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't very much better than that myself with that guard behind my back, who was quite jittery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was just as scared as they were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand, sir.

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the first time I -- this was the first time I encountered any prisoners, and I really can't say more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's what I'm saying. You can't tell us any more than you observed that they were scared, and you are an official responsible for security. Thank you very much. Any questions from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I have one, Your Honours, a follow-up to Judge Harhoff's question where he asked the witness whether the intelligence service interviewed the prisoner, and what the witness said. I would like to refer back to Exhibit 595, if I may. If the witness could be shown 595, just the first page, I'll wait for the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: The first full sentence, sir, of the body of the document says: "The 35th Ground Force Division, Military Security Division, Security Organ, in the interview with captured aggressor soldiers, obtained the following information and data." So, when Judge Harhoff was asking you questions, does this refresh your memory, that it was your organ that interviewed these witnesses and not the intelligence organ?

utterances.speaker: FADIL IMAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I don't remember this information, and I can't tell you who talked to these prisoners. At least based on this document, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Sartorio. Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions for the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic. Sir, that brings us to the conclusion of your testimony. Thank you for having come here to testify. You are excused. You may stand down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I make a suggestion, that we take our next break at this point in time and then we convene at 12.15 and sit through for a full 90 minutes with the following witness, if that would be acceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sit for 90 minutes with the following witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, so we have a full go. Ms. Sartorio will lead the witness. It might be preferable to go straightforward with a full 90 minutes, which would then take us to 1345.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure whether the recording or the interpreters, whoever it is, are able to go to sit for 90 minutes at a go. We'll have to find out about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have any contribution to make on that suggestion, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not at all, Your Honours. We agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. We will then sit 90 minutes later. Court adjourned. Come back at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could we move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I'll be directing this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I believe he needs to take the oath, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. May you please make the declaration, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, please tell us your full name.

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: My name is Alija, Ismet. "Alija" is my family name, and my first name is "Ismet."

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: What is your date of birth, sir?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: I was born on the 20th of June, 1959.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And in what municipality and country do you live, currently reside?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: Novo Sarajevo Municipality, Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And what is your current occupation, sir?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: I work at a faculty.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, sir, were you a member of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina; and if so, would you please briefly tell the Chamber about your military experience, what positions you held, and the dates you held those positions?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: I was a member of the BH Army, that's true, between the 10th of April, 1992 and my retirement in 2004. Throughout that time, the BH Army was transformed into the Federation Army, and then eventually it was named "The Armed Forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina." As for my posts, duties, I was in operations and training organ attached to the regional staff of the Territorial Defence between the 10th of April and sometime around the 1st of September, 1992. After that, the 1st Corps had just been set up. I was appointed the head of the operations and training organ of the 1st Corps. I remained in that position until - I can't remember exactly how long - but I think sometime around July 1993. I was then appointed Chief of Staff of the 1st Corps, and I remained in that position until the end of October 1993. From the 1st of November, give or take a day or two, I was deputy commander of the 6th Corps. I remained in that position until February 1994. After that, I became deputy commander of the 4th Corps. I remained in that position until February 1995. After that, I was head of the Department for Operative Planning, and I remained in that position until June 1997. After that, I became the BH's military attache to Turkey, and I remained in that position until 2000. In 2000, I, again, became head of the Operations Department. I remained in that position until 2002. Between 2002 and my retirement in 2004, I was Chief of Staff for Training -- for Training and Doctrine. Those were my duties in the BH Army. I must point out again, for a while it, became the Army of the Federation, and then it was eventually named "the Armed Forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina." So it went through several transformations throughout this time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, for that detailed and comprehensive answer about your military background. I would like to concentrate our questions on the time period in which you said that you were head of the Department for Operative Planning; and, particularly, we're going to concentrate on the spring and summer of 1995. Tell us, what is the Department for Operative Planning? What was it then?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: Are you referring to 1995 to 1996, that time interval?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes. I'm actually limiting the time frame between April of 1995 and October of 1995. What function did the Department for Operative Planning serve, and what level was it on in terms of the whole administration?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: The Operative Planning Department was comprised within the Operative Planning Administration. It is one of its departments. Its duty was to monitor the situation in the theatre of war, to analyse it, to submit proposals to the head of the administration, to draw up individual documents on the orders of the head of the administration, to draw up certain orders, to prepare monthly, quarterly, and annual coordination plans.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I please interrupt. Sir, do you have a piece of paper before you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do have one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you reading from it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a lot of papers in front of me, as I am consulting them, but I don't have to, if I cannot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The idea here, sir, is that you try and testify from memory. So to the extent that you may need to refresh your memory from documents, we've got to be aware of that. Thank you so much. Yes, Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. First of all, let's talk about the Operative Planning Administration; and, in this regard, I'd like to show you a diagram that we looked at during proofing, so that you can put this administration into context for the Chamber; and then I want to talk to you specifically about the Operative Planning Department of that administration so that -- because, otherwise, there may be confusion for the rest of the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So may the witness please be shown P01839, and I actually have hard copies of the organisational chart in both B/C/S and English because it may not be easy to read on the screen, if that would be acceptable. It's toward the end of the document, which, again, I'd prefer to put the plan on the ELMO. I think it would be a lot easier. Thank you. The translation -- unfortunately, the translation copy into English doesn't look like this, and it's more of -- more boxes, not organised. So I think we'll have to suffice with the B/C/S version and ask the witness to identify the different departments, if he may. Would that be acceptable?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Proceed, Madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, using this diagram, the president is at the top, the Presidency; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let the witness testify.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: At the very top in the middle, could you show us where the Presidency level is on this diagram?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ask him what it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise this diagram?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: Yes. I do recognise this diagram, although I haven't seen it very often.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this diagram at least purports to be, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: This is a diagram of the structure of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can you point out and put a number -- you can write on the ELMO with a pen, if you would - if the usher may help the witness - where the Presidency is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Don't testify. Let him point out for us, and let him tell us what he sees. Don't tell him what it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. I'm trying to save time because I'm not sure this is contested, in terms of this, but I don't want to ask him about every single box on this diagram because that will take all day. So I'm just trying to -- this is for an illustration so the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just ask him, "What is that box, the top-most box?" Let him tell us what it is, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, what is the top-most box, please?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: The top-most box is the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Could you put a "1" on that box, please?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the box below it, could you tell us what that box is?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: That is the Supreme Command Staff, which is headed by a commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Number 2, please.

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That "2" looks like a "1."

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Could you make that a little more clear, sir, the "2"? Who is the commander at this point, at this level, sir?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: [Marks] I'm not quite sure what the date of this diagram is because the first commander was Sefer Halilovic, who then was the Chief of Staff, and the commandership was assumed by Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm hearing some echo somewhere. I don't know whether I'm the only one. Can we ask them to keep quiet and talk a little further away?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Security?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, my questions are limited, unless I specify differently, from April to October of 1995. So who was the commander at that level at that time?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: Yes. I understand you completely, but then this scheme is not okay, because it says the Staff of the Supreme Command; and in the interval which you referred to, according to my information, the commander was General Rasim Delic. But I should like to emphasise that this diagram, which you have given me, is not clear sufficiently.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, why don't you tell us what isn't clear about this diagram.

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: It says here "the Staff of the Supreme Command," and below it is the General Staff of the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: What is your testimony as to what was contained in that box? What level, what persons?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: I would not comment on that. I'm just commenting on this particular diagram. The commander was General Delic, and the Chief of Staff was General Halilovic, Sefer Halilovic. As in this particular time the commander of the General Staff, General Rasim Delic, was the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, on this diagram, do you see the Operations Planning Administration?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Could you put a number "3" by that?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And to whom did this administration report directly to?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: The administration reported to the Staff, to the Chief of Staff, to the Staff of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, headed by the Chief of Staff; so directly to the Chief of Staff, who is here, this person. [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Could you put a "4" there, please, and tell us who that person was from April to October of 1995?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: [Marks] The Chief of Staff was General Enver Hadzihasanovic at the time, and Brigadier-General Asim Dzambasovic was the head of administration.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, within the administration, you mentioned that you were head of the, I believe you said, Operative Planning Department; is that correct? I believe that's what you said.

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: Yes. This administration has its elements, its structural units. One of them is here, and also here, the Department for Operative Planning, which would be somewhere around here. [Indicates] I was the Chief of that unit, of that department.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So for this box, could you put a number "5." Is that box one department or several departments?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: [Marks] Number 5 stands for one department.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: That was the department of which you were the chief?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Sorry. Was there also another name for the Operative Planning Department at the time?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: No. As far as I can recall, no, there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: We'll see some documents. Okay. Now, what were your duties as Chief of the Operative Planning Department?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: My duties were the daily monitoring of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Daily monitoring of what, the situation?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: Of the situation at the front by way of reports which came in -- which came to the Operations Centre; analyses of the situation, consummate with the reports that arrived at the Operations Centre; writing specific documents and orders on the orders of the head of the administration; the drawing up of monthly, quarterly, and annual plans; the preparation of coordination plans; and other daily activities concerning the work of this particular department, falling within its ambit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And where was the Operative Centre located? It was within the administration, so where physically was this entity located?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: This body was part of this department. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: What do you mean by "this body"? That's your Operative Centre right there you just indicated?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: I have just drawn in, as part of this department, there was an Operations Centre. So we have the administration, department, centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And you were the deputy of the department, correct, which is number 5? I see the Judges --

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: No. I was the chief, the head of that department.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: All right. Sir, I want to make the diagram clear for the record. So number 3 represents or what is the full name of that agency or entity?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: That is the Operative Planning Administration.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And what is the full name of number 5?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: Operative Planning Department. Operative Planning Department is the full name. Could I please hear the English interpretation, because I see that we need to make a distinction between "administration" and "department." So "administration" is the administration, and "department" is the "odeljenje" or "department." Administration is the "uprava" or "administration." As part, within the department, we had the Operations or Operative Centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And who was in charge of the Operative Centre?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: I need a translation, please. Am I to follow proceedings in English or in Bosnian? Can I have the text? Heading the Operations Centre was Brigadier-General [as interpreted] Tabakovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Were you his --

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: Not "Brigadier-General" but "Brigadier."

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Just because so we don't cause more confusion, I'd like to use some abbreviations for the rest of the questions. So we will use the word "department" to represent the department of which you are the chief, and then the "Operative Centre." We will refer to those two names. Where, physically, were these entities located?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: Physically, they were located in the Operative Planning Administration.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: In what municipality or town, sir?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: In that time frame, they were in Kakanj Municipality, in a town called Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, I presume, were you in an office building in Kakanj?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't exactly call it an office building. It was a building which provided normal conditions for such an administration or department and centre to function normally.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And who else had rooms or offices at the department?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: I had my offices in the department, my desk officers also had their offices, and the head of the Operative Centre also had his office there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Who else, sir?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: Are you talking about the department or beyond that?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Beyond that, at the administration, who had offices in the administration?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: Brigadier Dzambasovic had his offices in the administration.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Were all these offices in the same building. The administration offices and the department offices and the Operative Centre offices, were they all in the same building?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: They were all in the same building, apart from the Operative Centre, which was detached.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Were there any offices maintained by any of the General Staff in this building?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: The office of General Hadzihasanovic, the cabinet of the Chief of Staff office was there, and there was a smaller room there to which would come General Delic sometimes for longer periods of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, where was General Delic's office in relation to General Hadzihasanovic's office?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: I think it was adjacent to it, to his office or cabinet, large office. General Hadzihasanovic had a cabinet-type office, and this here was a smaller room to which General Delic came only very seldom.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And where was your office in relation to the two generals' offices?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: It was in the same corridor, but some two or three doors or offices away from it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, in the spring and summer of 1995, did you see General Hadzihasanovic at the building in his office?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Can you tell us how often you saw him there?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: Very often, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And did you see General Delic there during that time frame?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: I did, but only very seldom.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Was there a period of time where you saw him more frequently than other times?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: Only during the Sarajevo operation, I saw him more frequently; but until that time, very infrequently.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And what time frame was this Sarajevo operation that you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: I cannot recall the exact date, but it was in 1995. Now, whether it was in July or August or September, I cannot say with precision, but it was sometime around that period in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And when you say you saw him "more frequently," can you be more specific as to that term, "more frequently"? What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: Well, during the Sarajevo operation, we had specific teams at the Operations Centre. General Delic would drop in, come by to see how this was functioning, and that was the time when I saw him more frequently.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you to just explain briefly what the role was for the Department for Operations and Planning during the combat operations in 1995.

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: Which operations?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, were there operations in 1995?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, the Sarajevo operation took place, at the end of which was an operation to lift the siege from the city of Sarajevo, and I can talk about that operation if that is what you want me to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: We'll be showing -- I'll be showing you some documents, sir, and we'll be getting into the different operations in more detail. But what I'm asking is: What function did the department play in military operations?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: As I said at the outset, the department monitored the situation along the front line through reports that the department was receiving from its subordinate units, the various corps above all. Based on those reports, the duty officer, who was at the Operations Centre, conducted an analysis, drafted a report, and then dispatched this report to a number of addressees. At the morning briefing, this officer would inform the Chief of Staff, first and foremost, because normally he would chair the briefing whenever he could, or the head of the administration; and based on that, certain tasks would be handed out as to what measures were to be taken. Most of the matters would be dealt with at this briefing. The General Staff would hand out tasks and duties and responsibilities, and said who was to report on what. That was the major part of our tasks, so much for those reports that were being sent to the Operations Centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And I'm going to ask you to go back to the diagram, if you would.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: If we may see the diagram again.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, could you tell us, when you say -- okay. Did the Department for Operative Planning, you mentioned that it received information. From whom did it receive information?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: The Department for Operative Planning was receiving orders from the head of the administration. The Operations Centre, on the other hand, was receiving reports from subordinate units, the corps. The Operations Centre was receiving those, and the department was receiving orders from the head of the administration, Brigadier Dzambasovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And could you point out, on the diagram, where the corps are represented here, if they are?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, 6th, 7th Corps. [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: That's fine for the transcript, but could you just make a circle around those and mark those as number 6, so those are the corps. Just one big circle around all of the boxes.

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, would the corps report to you or to your department, submit reports to your department; and if so, how frequently?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: They did not submit reports to me, nor was I at a sufficient level of command and control, within the command-and-control system, for them to submit reports to me. It was based on orders, they submitted reports to the Operations Centre in relation to the Kakanj command post.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: But being the Chief for Operative Planning, were you also over the Operations Centre?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: The Operations Centre was part of the Department for Operative Planning. The head of that department was one of my subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So reports would come in to the Operations Centre from the corps; correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And how often would these reports come in?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: There were daily reports, regular reports, and interim reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And we're going to look at some of those reports in just a few minutes. Now, where would the corps get --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. Can I just get clarity.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. Could I please get clarity. You know, a little earlier, Madam Sartorio, you asked the witness whether the corps submitted reports to him, and he said they did not and that he was not of a sufficient level of command and control, within the command-and-control system, for them to submit reports to him. Now he is saying the corps reported to, in fact, his subordinate. I'm not quite sure I understand what is happening here now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I'll ask some more questions, Your Honour, and try and get clarification.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: The corps would submit daily reports. I think you just said that; correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And to what entity would these daily reports be submitted?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: They were in relation to the command post in Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Is that -- is the command post another way of discussing the Operations Centre?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: No, no. The command post is a more general concept. A command post comprises everything that there was in Kakanj at that command post, starting with the Chief of Staff, all the administrations that were there. The command post comprised, included all of that. So if a report was submitted to the command post, the report was to reach whoever was responsible at the command post, in this case the Chief of Staff, General Hadzihasanovic. Now, there is one thing that we must clarify for the benefit of the Chamber. Reports were being received because they were being sent to the Operations Centre. There was a duty officer there who would go through all of these incoming reports, and there were dozens of those, running into 30 or 40 pages each; and then the operations duty officer would draw up a brief report for the Presidency, the commander, and whoever else was there, the Administration for Moral Guidance, the superior command. The reports in their entirety would be forwarded to the post in Kakanj, the person in charge; and, in this case, it was General Hadzihasanovic. But, and I must say this again, this was a lot of paper, and General Hadzihasanovic would not have been able to read all of this, and all the other subordinate officers. So the duty officer would draw up a brief report. At a briefing, he would inform the Staff about the situation along the front lines. General Hadzihasanovic would be there. When he wasn't, Brigadier Dzambasovic would stand in for him; and then this report would be submitted to the Presidency and all the other relevant addressees. Certain --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have just -- do you want to finish your sentence?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: No, no, it's fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Why don't we go into the documents. Now, the corps -- would the corps receive information from subunits; and if so, could you please explain briefly how that system operated, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: Well, I know, or at least I think I know, the first report in the unit would be produced by the company. The company would then forward this - if I may just read the English - would then forward this to the battalion. The battalion would then forward this to the brigade. Whoever was responsible for this in the brigade would process this and send it on to the division corps, and then the corps would dispatch this to us at the Kakanj command centre. It would be received by the Operations Centre, and the duty officer would get all these reports from all the corps in the units. He would analyse these, and based on these, produce a brief report. What's the point of the whole exercise? If you start with the company and go all the way up to the General Staff, that would amount to at least 300 different separate reports, and I was supposed to produce a half page or a page, at the very most, based on these 300 reports for the General Staff. So you have a whole network of reporting, producing this one brief report. It was sent to the Presidency, to the commander, and whoever the other relevant addressees were, the Moral Guidance Administration, the Logistics Centre and so on and so forth. That's how they were informed about the situation that at certain times prevailed along the front line.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, you mentioned a short while ago that there were daily briefings. Could you please explain who attended these briefings and what information was discussed at these briefings? The types of information, I should say.

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: As I said, at these briefings, there would normally be the Chief of Staff, General Hadzihasanovic. A duty officer would briefly brief everyone on the situation, based on reports. If he wasn't there, and sometimes he was busy elsewhere, Brigadier Dzambasovic would stand in for him. And then based on this report, all those who were present at the command post in Kakanj, in addition to the administrations that made up the Staff, there would be the sections from the security organ, the intelligence organ, the Moral Guidance Administration, and so on and so forth. Those people were normally present, so that orders could be issued on the spot. For the most part, the Chief of Staff would get most of the work done during this time. He would issue an order, and we would all leave and continue going about our different jobs; or, alternatively, it could have been done by Brigadier Dzambasovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: May the witness be shown P02232.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do that, ma'am, what are you going to do with this diagram, number one; and, number two, before you called this diagram, you called "P01839." I don't know what you intend to do with all these documents. This document here, I would like to see the little box beneath box number 5 being given a name and a number.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, could you mark, on the ELMO with the pen, in the box number 5 what that box is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Not in the box in number 5. Under number 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Under number 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The little box.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: What is the little box under number 5? Just write it out, please.

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: This one, this is the Operations Centre. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Well, Your Honour, may the witness be shown the whole document, P01839, because there are several pages to this. This is just one page of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This document?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, at this point, I would tender this separately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. The organogram on the ELMO is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 597.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May the witness now be shown P02232.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Be what are you doing with P01839?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I'm not doing -- I'm not admitting it in evidence, Your Honour. Just the chart is all I want to admit at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Now you want P02232?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes. The first page is fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, sir, can you tell us what this document is?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: This is a regular log, a combat report; a regular daily combat report.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And it's a combat report from whom to whom?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: 328th or 329th - I can't see clearly - Mountain Brigade is submitting this to the 35th Division.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, in terms of -- where would this information go after it went to the 35th Division?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: This is the 35th Division --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, leading question. First of all, one should ascertain whether it would be sent anywhere at all, and then perhaps ask where to.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I'll rephrase that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, sir, this says "Regular Daily Combat Report" from the 328th Mountain Brigade to the 35th Division. Now, what would be done with this report, if anything, at the 35th Division?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: I can comment to the following extent: This is a regular daily combat report sent by the 328th Brigade to the 35th Division. Now, what did the Division do with this? I can't say, simply because I don't know what they did with it, if anything. What they wrote, based on this, the document doesn't show that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: That's fair, sir. And I understand you can't say exactly what happened, but what were the procedures? Because you're in the Operations Centre and you are tasked with writing reports that go above you, what were the procedures when a report was filed by a brigade to a division, from the division to the corps, from the corps to the Operations Centre? Just walk us through the procedures, please.

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: I did just this about ten minutes ago. There would be an initial report, sometimes an oral report, and this was produced by the company. That is the lowest-ranking unit or one of the lower-ranking units. After the company, the report would be received by the battalion. Three or four reports by companies are submitted to the battalion. The duty officer in the battalion reads these reports and sums it up, makes a summary report based on these. But one thing that one needs to keep in mind is that at this level of reporting, we had people who weren't trained properly, stone masons, carpenters, sometimes locksmiths, those kind of people. And after that --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: May I just finish, please, since you asked the question, after all? Once these reports reach the battalion, the company reports, the duty officer in the battalion would analyse these; and then depending on his level of training and education, he would try to single out what was particularly important. He would do his best. Whatever he produced would then reach the brigade, and the duty officer at the brigade level would look at what the duty officer in the battalion had written. What exactly he wrote would be based on purely subjective assessments which very much depended on his level of general education, military training, civilian education, and so on and so forth. I'm just trying to put you in the picture so that the Chamber might understand. We didn't have properly-trained officers, especially at lower levels; semi-literate sometimes, I could even go as far as to say that. The battalion would then finish their reports, and the three or four battalion reports would eventually reach the brigade. The 328th Brigade specifically produced this report based on 15 reports received by the companies and three or four by the battalions; and whoever the duty officer happened to be, depending on his training, on his level of education, he drafted this report. This was sent to the 35th Division. Now, what did the Division do? As a matter of principle, that's what I'm saying. I don't know about this particular report. But as a matter of principle, according to military doctrine, the method of reporting and the principle of subordination, they would have had to inform the corps, as a matter of principle. But, again, I have to express my reservations about this particular report. This particular report, I have nowhere -- I have no idea where it was sent to; therefore, I can't comment. As a matter of principle, and this is another segment of reporting, this report was to be submitted to the corps, and the corps was to present its own summary, its own brief report, and dispatch it to the Kakanj command post, which is where the Operations Centre was that we have already referred to more than once. After all of these reports were received from the corps-level units, one would draw up a summary report, and this would then be dispatched to all the addressees that I've mentioned and pointed out already. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. We may put this document away, Your Honours, and I'd like the witness to be shown --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're not tendering it in?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, we'll ask that it be tendered in evidence, but I know if the Defence is objecting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour. There is absolutely no foundation for this document to be admitted, at least not in relation to this particular witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour. I don't want to press it. There are more important documents. It was for illustrative purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Then the document is not tendered.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes. P02130, please, may it be shown the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, could you tell us what this document is?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: It says that this is an analysis of the strategic attack, Proljece-95. The period covered is between the 6th of May and the 31st of May, 1995. It was produced by the 35th Division Command and dispatched to the 3rd Corps Command.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, are you familiar with Operation Proljece?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Do you recall seeing any reports, being the Chief of the Department for Operative Planning, about this operation?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: This may have been referred to in the 3rd Corps report, the name itself, but my memory of that operation is very scarce. I may have seen a reference to it of some sort in a 3rd Corps report, but I don't remember any particulars.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like you to look about halfway down the body of the document, I where it discusses: "After the preparations and reports."

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Bring the English document up.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: If you could read that one very long sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where is it in the English, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: "After the Preparations," it's about the 3rd sentence. Can you see it now, if you can highlight? Right there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: If you could read that sentence, sir, I'd like to ask you if you are familiar with any of the specifics of this operation. It may not be by name, but are you familiar with the El Mujahedin participating in an operation in June 1995?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: As I said, I don't remember. This was a long time in some report that the corps submitted to us at the General Staff. I read some reference to Proljece-95, but I know exactly nothing about that operation. This is a report by the 35th Division, submitted to the 3rd Corps; therefore, I'd like to ask you one thing. I know nothing about this. I am not qualified to talk about this document. You have the Division, you have the Corps. I can talk about documents that were submitted to the General Staff, the Operations Centre, which was a place that I had access to. This is about something between the Division and the Corps. Unless I really have to, I would decline any offer to discuss this. I'm simply not familiar with this document, and it didn't have anything to do with me, specifically. I was back at the General Staff, or rather, at the Staff, in the Operations Centre. I wasn't attached to the 3rd Corps or the Division in question. Therefore, if we could please refrain from discussing this, unless I really have no choice. If you absolutely want me to say something about it, perhaps I can say something about it in purely technical terms.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, yes. The point of this document is to show the reporting procedures, that the previous document was reporting from a brigade to a division. Is this document reporting from a division to the Corps?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: The 35th Division Command - that's what it says - submitted this analysis to the 3rd Corps. That's what the document reflects, what I can see.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: We'll move on, Your Honour. This document may be put away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That document is put away.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: May the witness be shown document 2193.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it a "P0"" document?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, P02193.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, are you able to identify this document?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: Yes. This is a regular daily combat report sent by the 3rd Corps Command to the General Staff of the Armed Forces of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, at the Kakanj command post, and to another two addresses.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And could you identify, please, for the record, the date of this document?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: Zenica, the 29th of June, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: May we go to the last page of the document so we can see the name.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, do you know whose name that is at the end of the document?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: At the bottom of the page, it is written "Colonel Ekrem Alihodzic."

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And do you know who he is and what position he held, if any?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: I do not know Ekrem Alihodzic well. I did not know him well, as he was in the 3rd Corps, but I had heard about that person. While he was at that post, I believe that he worked in the Corps Command, in the security organ. I believe so, but I cannot claim it. This is an incomplete document because you cannot see, on the left-hand side, who wrote the document. These initials only indicated the typist, but not the author of the document, so I believe the document to be incomplete.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I'd like to draw your attention to the section, on the English, it's page 35, and it's discussing the 35th Division.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: In The B/C/S, it is page 2 at the top, page 3 in English. That's the B/C/S. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So, in this report, sir, to the Kakanj command post from the 3rd Corps, this is reporting on the activities of the 35th Division?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And if you look down further toward the end of the section, it starts out: "In the 35 Ground Forces Division." Do you see that section? Can you tell us what that section is about, sir?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: The 35th Division was undertaking defensive operations in its zone of responsibility. It was defending itself against -- from the aggressor. The focus of the engagement of our forces is on defence -- the defence of the city of Maglaj. So all the defences were concentrated on the city of Maglaj, and also the engineering works. The reconnaissance of the forward end was also one of the focuses of activities of the aggressor's forces, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I'm asking specifically about that one section about the El Mujahedin, and I want you to -- at least in the English version, I want you to explain to us what that is a reference to. What is the El Mujahedin doing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It says "El Mudjahedin Detachment."

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: "Detachment." Yes, sorry. Thank you, Your Honour, for correcting that.

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: Could I just have the context, please? Let me just get the context. I'm reading from the top. For the continuation of operations and within the Operation Proljece-95, one combatant was lightly wounded -- severely wounded and three lightly. Preparation of combatants for the forthcoming combat activities, together with the El Mudjahedin Detachment. This says that the 35th Division will train and prepare combatants for the upcoming combat operations, together with the El Mujahid department. This means that, as a military specialist, this is how I would analyse it: There is the Division on the one side and on the other the detachment. There are two components. The 35th Division will train and prepare combatants together with this other component, which is the El Mudjahedin Detachment. This is the way I would analyse it, Your Honours; namely, that there would be preparation and training of fighters in this way.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, we would ask this document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 598.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, sir, in addition to daily reports, did the Operations Centre receive other types of reports?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: The Operations Centre did not. The Operations Centre only received regular combat reports and daily reports. All other reports would be dispatched along another line to the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And where was the -- was the Chief of Staff physically located in Kakanj?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: The Chief of Staff was in the building which I referred to earlier. He was in a building that had been adapted to control-and-command purposes. If you have the diagram, I can show you on it where the Chief of Staff was. Actually, the Operations Centre was elsewhere, across the street from that building, perhaps some 100 metres away from it; that is to say, the Communications Centre was some 100 metres away from the Chief of Staff, and it was to the Communications Centre that all other acts and documents came which would later be dispatched towards the Chief of Staff. These were other documents, you know. There was a series of different documents, and the daily combat reports and interim reports came through the Operations Centre. All the other documents went to the Chief of Staff, who would then initial them and assign the different tasks to their different -- to different people to carry them out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In which town, sir, was the office of the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, from your previous answer, you said there were a series of different documents. The daily combat reports and the interim reports came through the Operations Centre. So that went back to my original question about whether there were any other reports, and you're just telling me now you said "interim." Were there any type of monthly reports that would come to the Operations Centre?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: There were monthly reports, but I should like to emphasise again, because I want to be very clear, daily combat reports and special or interim combat reports arrived at the Operations Centre. An entire series, a multitude of other documents, which concerned the issues of logistics, morals, different branches, communications, different branches, artillery, armour, armoured units, ABH units, visits, requests for the Chief of Staff to receive the president of the municipality, and a multitude of other reports and documents went from the Communications Centre to the Chief of Staff directly, who at the time was General Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. May the witness now be shown P02196.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us what this document is?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: This is a plan, a coordination of the General Staff of the Bosnia-Herzegovina Army for the month of July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And does it say "Kakanj, July 1995"?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: It says for the month of July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Can we move down the page, please, and the B/C/S. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Does that say "Kakanj," sir?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: Yes, it does, it says so.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Was this document received at the Department of Operations and Planning?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: This document was not received in Operations and Planning, but Operations and Planning actively participated in its production. It was an active participant in its making.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And do you see, in the upper left-hand corner, who has endorsed this plan?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, the plan is seven pages long, at least in English. Can you tell us, in general, what this plan is?

utterances.speaker: ISMET ALIJA
utterances.text: This is a coordination plan. So to latch onto the first question, a global order regulated that all subordinated units, meaning the Corps and the administrations, would submit once monthly a report on their activities for the coordination plan, which was drawn up every month. What did this imply? Every subordinated unit and administration was to submit its activities; namely, the activities it planned to undertake during the month that would follow, on the basis of all the reports which came to the Chief of Staff. He would of course assign them to whoever he thought was to carry out the assignment. In this particular case, it was the Operations and Training Department and administration. So a team composed from representatives of all the administrations would draw up a consolidated plan of all activities. For instance, if training in the Training Centre in Zenica was planned for that month, all the corps had to send their officers or men to the Training Centre in Zenica on a particular date; or if there was some other activity, it would be thus coordinated. Joint activities were coordinated under the coordination plan.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, we ask that this document be admitted in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 599.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: It looks like our time is up, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sir, we haven't finished. We will come back tomorrow at quarter to 2:00 in the afternoon -- I beg your pardon, quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon, in this same courtroom tomorrow. Court adjourned to quarter past 2.00 tomorrow in Courtroom II.
